title: AMD Cannot Catch Nvidia, But It Sure Can Make Some Money
gist: Timothy Prickett Morgan argues AMD is hurting Intel far more than Nvidia because HBM allocations from Samsung, SK Hynix and Micron cap its Instinct GPU output, and consensus has the Nvidia-AMD revenue gap staying near 6.7x through 2029. AMD's Q3 2026 revenue rose 44.7% to $13.38B with Data Center up 96.9% to $8.55B, Epyc CPUs (est. $4.68B) still outselling Instinct GPUs (est. $3.43B), and Lisa Su guiding to server revenue doubling in 2027 and datacenter exceeding 80% of revenue.

themes.theme: HBM supply caps AMD's GPU share

insights.claim: The author argues AMD is hurting Intel far more than Nvidia, mainly because AMD cannot obtain more HBM allocations from Samsung, SK Hynix and Micron to build more Instinct GPUs.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: HBM supply, not demand or architecture, is the gating factor for AMD's AI GPU upside; HBM makers hold pricing power.
insights.quote: AMD cannot make more Instinct GPUs because it cannot get more HBM allocations from Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron

insights.claim: AMD ships fewer GPUs than it could because the Instinct MI400 series carries much more HBM per GPU than Nvidia's Blackwell B200/B300 and Rubin R200, which the author says are intentionally under-memoried to maximize accelerator volumes.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Memory-per-GPU design choices trade unit volume for performance balance, limiting AMD unit share under fixed HBM supply.
insights.locator: But let’s be honest. AMD is hurting

insights.claim: The author estimates AMD's Q3 2026 Instinct GPU sales at $3.43 billion, up 72.3%, and says AMD could sell 5x, possibly 10x, that amount with more memory allocations and packaging capacity.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Implies large latent AI GPU demand for AMD that is unlocked only by HBM and advanced-packaging supply.
insights.quote: If AMD had 5X times the memory allocations and could line up the packaging for more GPUs, do I think it could sell them? Abso-freaking-lutely.

insights.claim: The author proposes that AMD's Instinct MI500 use optical interposers and disaggregated, composable HBM on trays so memory can be reused as GPUs are swapped, which he says could give AMD an architectural edge over Nvidia's static configurations, though he doubts it will happen.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Flags memory disaggregation as a possible competitive lever given extreme DRAM costs.

insights.claim: Nvidia's revenue lead over AMD grew from 1.64x in 2021 ($26.9B vs $16.4B) to 2.69x in 2023 ($60.9B vs $22.7B) and an expected 6.79x in 2026 (about $354B vs $52.2B).
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Quantifies Nvidia's dominance; AMD is not closing the gap despite AI growth.
insights.locator: In 2021, a year before the GenAI boom

insights.claim: One Wall Street consensus estimate, shown in Marvell's charts justifying its $115 billion acquisition of Lumentum, has Nvidia at $1,091 billion revenue in calendar 2029 versus $164 billion for AMD, a 6.65x gap essentially unchanged from 2026.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Consensus assumes AMD grows in line with Nvidia but never gains relative share; also notes a major Marvell-Lumentum optical deal.
insights.locator: In 2021, a year before the GenAI boom

insights.claim: The author attributes part of Nvidia's lead to AMD not owning the most lucrative AI networking segments (scale-across, scale-out and scale-up).
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Networking attach is a key Nvidia moat and revenue multiplier AMD lacks.
insights.locator: In 2021, a year before the GenAI boom

insights.claim: The author argues the AI market is underserved rather than truly competitive, giving vendors pricing power and prompting hyperscalers, cloud builders and big model builders to design cheaper, specialized in-house compute engines.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Supply-constrained AI market supports margins for all vendors while fueling custom-silicon demand.
insights.quote: the AI market is not really competitive as much as it is underserved, which always gives pricing power to the vendors

insights.claim: AMD's Q3 2026 revenue rose 44.7% to $13.38 billion, operating income rose 2.2x to $2.83 billion, and net income rose 95.3% to $2.43 billion (18.2% of revenue), while cash more than doubled to $15.78 billion.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Strong margin expansion and balance sheet as Helios rack costs roll off.
insights.locator: In Q3, AMD’s revenues were up

insights.claim: AMD's Data Center group revenue rose 96.9% to $8.55 billion, beating its 'more than 80 percent' growth target, with operating income up 2.7x to $2.88 billion, and datacenter now two-thirds of revenue.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: AMD is now primarily a datacenter company, re-rating its earnings mix.
insights.locator: Data Center group revenues were $8.55 billion

insights.claim: The author estimates AMD's Epyc CPU sales at $4.68 billion in Q3 2026, up 116%, with hyperscaler/cloud CPU sales up 2.2x to $3.53 billion and enterprise and other up 105% to $1.15 billion, making CPUs the majority of datacenter revenue for a third straight quarter.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Server CPU demand, including for agentic AI, is a major and underappreciated AMD growth driver.
insights.locator: In the Data Center group, it was once again

insights.claim: AMD holds a little more than a third of X86 server CPU shipments and a little less than half of revenues in the first half of 2026, gaining share from Intel through better product, process and packaging supply, and higher ASPs.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Continued structural share loss for Intel in the most profitable CPU segment.
insights.locator: No one is expecting such a thing

insights.claim: AMD's non-datacenter segments diverged in Q3 2026: Client revenue rose 7.2% to $2.95 billion, Gaming fell 40.4% to $773 million, and Embedded (Xilinx FPGAs) rose 29.4% to $1.11 billion with operating income up 60.1% to $453 million.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Embedded FPGA recovery is a margin contributor while gaming GPUs are now immaterial.
insights.locator: AMD’s Client group, which sells CPUs

insights.claim: Venice Epyc processors began shipping for revenue in Q3 2026 with 240 OEM/ODM platforms in development, 20% more design wins than Turin, and Helios racks with MI455X GPUs have started shipping to Meta Platforms, Microsoft, OpenAI and Oracle.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Named hyperscaler and AI-lab customers validate AMD's rack-scale AI platform.

insights.claim: Lisa Su guided that AMD's datacenter AI business will grow 50% sequentially in Q4 2026, pushing GPU sales above CPU sales, and that 2026 datacenter revenue will be more than double 2025.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Signals a sharp Q4 Instinct ramp as Helios enters production workloads.
insights.locator: Looking ahead, Su said that AMD

insights.claim: Su said customers expanded Epyc and Instinct deployment plans and AMD secured more supply, so it now expects server revenue to double in 2027, datacenter AI revenue to beat its prior projection, and datacenter to exceed 80% of total revenue in 2027.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Raised 2027 visibility supports upward estimate revisions for AMD.
insights.quote: We now expect server revenue to double year-over-year in 2027 and datacenter AI revenue to grow even faster than we projected 90 days ago.
